seoDescription: Discover the power of Aspect-Oriented Programming in this beginner-friendly Spring AOP tutorial. Learn how to separate cross-cutting concerns, such as logging, security, and transaction management, from your core business logic to create cleaner, more maintainable code. This practical example walks you through creating an Aspect class, defining Advice with @Before, and specifying a Pointcut to inject behavior automatically. Understand the key concepts and annotations like @Aspect, @Component, and @EnableAspectJAutoProxy.

chapters.description: This chapter introduces AOP as the solution, defining an "Aspect" as a class that modularizes cross-cutting concerns like logging and security.

chapters.description: This segment demonstrates how to add the necessary JAR files for Spring AOP and use the `@Aspect` annotation to designate a class as an aspect.

chapters.description: This final chapter covers the last steps: adding the `@Component` annotation to the aspect and enabling AOP with `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy` to make the full example work.

summary:
## The Problem: Cross-Cutting Concerns

- Business logic in methods often gets mixed with other responsibilities.
- **Examples**: Logging, security checks, and transaction management.
- This leads to **code duplication** across multiple methods and makes the core business logic harder to read and maintain.

## The Solution: Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP)

AOP provides a way to separate (or modularize) these **cross-cutting concerns** from the primary business logic.

> [!NOTE]
> AOP is a **supplement** to Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), not a replacement. It helps make OOP code cleaner.

## Key AOP Concepts

- **Aspect**: A class that encapsulates cross-cutting concerns. It is marked with the `@Aspect` annotation.
- **Advice**: The action to be taken (the "what"). It's a method within an aspect that runs at a particular point.
  - *Example Advice Types*: `@Before`, `@After`, `@Around`.
- **Pointcut**: An expression that defines where the advice should be applied (the "when" and "where"). It specifies the method(s) to be intercepted.
  - *Example Expression*: `execution(public void com.navin.Alien.show())`

## Implementing Spring AOP: Step-by-Step

Here is the process to implement AOP in a Spring project with Java Configuration.

1.  **Add Dependencies**:
    - Ensure you have the required AOP-specific JAR files in your project's build path. Standard Spring Core does not include them by default.

2.  **Create an Aspect Class**:
    - Create a class that will contain your advice logic.
    - Annotate it with `@Aspect` and `@Component` so Spring can discover and manage it as a bean.
    ```java
    @Aspect
    @Component
    public class Helper {
        // Advice methods go here
    }
    ```

3.  **Define an Advice and Pointcut**:
    - Inside your Aspect class, create a method for your concern (e.g., logging).
    - Annotate it with an advice type like `@Before`.
    - Provide a pointcut expression to target a specific method execution.
    ```java
    @Before("execution(public void com.navin.Alien.show())")
    public void log() {
        System.out.println("show called");
    }
    ```

4.  **Enable AOP in Configuration**:
    - In your main Spring configuration class (the one with `@Configuration`), add the `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy` annotation.

    > [!IMPORTANT]
    > Your AOP setup will not work without `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy`. This annotation tells Spring to find and process components with AOP annotations.

    ```java
    @Configuration
    @ComponentScan("com.navin")
    @EnableAspectJAutoProxy
    public class AppConfig {
        // ... Spring bean configurations
    }
    ```

## Result

The advice method (`log()`) will be executed automatically **before** the target method (`show()`) is called. The business logic class (`Alien`) remains "innocent" and completely unaware of the logging aspect, achieving a clean separation of concerns.

## Setting Up the Basic Spring Application

Welcome back, aliens. My name is Naveen Reddy, and in this video, we'll see an example of Spring AOP. So before going for AOP, you have to make sure that you know Spring Framework, at least the basics of it.

In the last video which I've uploaded, there is a video of Spring Framework. So you will find the video in the description area. If you have not seen that, do watch it. But if you already know Spring Framework, that's fine. I will explain the code to you and you're good to go.

So what I'm doing here is I'm trying to use—I have an Alien class here, a very simple class in which perhaps I have a method called `show()`. And I made this class as a component because I want to make this as a Spring bean, and that's how we do it, right? We simply write `@Component` which will make this class as a Spring bean class.

And so what I wanted is, I wanted the object of Alien here. So we got an object here. But instead of doing `Alien a1 = new Alien()`, normally that's how we do it in Java, right? But then, since Spring Framework says, "We will provide you with the objects, you don't have to make an object by yourself," we are doing this extra thing. This is the object of `ApplicationContext` which will help you to give the—which will help you with the object. You simply have to call this method, which is `getBean()`, by passing the type of a class of which you want an object. So we want an object of Alien, so we will get the object.

Now, where have I done the configuration for this? So there are multiple ways you can configure your Spring Framework. There are XML-based configuration, we can use annotations, or we can totally go for Java-based configuration. So I am using Java-based configuration here. So as you can see, I have a class, `AppConfig`, in which I'm not doing any configuration, and I'm asking Spring Framework to do everything for me. So just write `@Configuration` and `@ComponentScan` and by mentioning the package in which package you have all the components, it will do it for you. So as you can see, I have a main method here in which I am creating an object of Alien and then I'm calling `show()`. This is what is a normal Spring code example.

So before going for AOP, again, let me just run this code just to show you what we are expecting. So if I run this file, you can see we got the output, and the output is "Hello world." It's that simple.

## Identifying Cross-Cutting Concerns

But then, why do we need AOP? So let's go to this Alien here and think about this. If we talk about a method, this will be your business method, right? Normally we don't write a method which prints "Hello World," right? In a real-life scenario, we write lots of code. Example, let's say if you want to buy something online, or maybe if you want to create a method for that. Maybe you want to transfer money to someone. Maybe you want to check all the details about a customer. You want to check, you want to transfer all the assets from one department to another department. So normally you do all those things in a method, right? Now this method will have multiple statements, not like one statement here. It will have multiple statements. Let's say it has 15 statements.

Now 15 statements is something using which you can do all the tasks. Let's say you are transferring money, so all this thing will be mentioned here. Now this 15 statements is actually your business logic, because as a developer, our job is to convince on a business problem, right? So this is my business logic. So this is where I will write my business logic. So this 15 lines is business logic.

But what happens, you know? With this logic, we don't only write the logic. We also add some extra things. Example, whenever you call a method, we also maintain a log file, right? A log file will normally take two lines of code, maybe one line of code or two lines of code. So we maintain a log when you call a method, and we also maintain a log when you are done with the execution. So here also you will write two lines of code for log. Right? Again, if you know about different logging concepts, we can use log4j or whatever logging concept you use, or maybe tracing, so you normally do that. So in all the enterprise applications, we do maintain a log file when you call a method and when you're done with the method execution, because it will be helpful for you to debug your application later. Let's say if you have deployed your application on a server and something went wrong, how would you know what went wrong? And that's where log comes into picture, right? So you can debug your application there.

Now, we don't just write log files, we also write a security code. When I say security code, I simply mean, you know, when you are calling this method, you want to make sure that the user is logged in because I want to transfer money only when I'm logged into the system. So maybe one line of code you will check for the security, you will do some security stuff. Maybe one line of code or four lines of code, depending upon which security feature you are using, right? If you are using some APIs you can do it in one line. If you're doing it by yourself, maybe five to six lines, right? So that's one thing you will write.

Now we also have to do the transactions. Now whenever you work with databases or if you work with JNDI, maybe some—you have a database on some other server and if you are using some framework, so normally what we do is we maintain the transaction. Now what we do is, before executing your business logic, you have to start the transaction. Because of course, when you're transferring money you are doing a transaction, right? In that case, you begin the transaction. So here somewhere you will begin your transaction, right? And then at the end, once you complete your business logic, you will end your transaction here. So this is where your transaction gets terminated, or maybe you can say `commit`. Now this is where you will commit it, right? Okay.

Now, once you say begin and commit, so just see this, it may be one line of code, maybe five lines of code, you never know, right? So it may be one line of code here, maybe five lines of code. The thing is, if you are doing this code, I mean if you're writing your method, you have 15 lines of code which is actually your business logic, and apart from that, you have so many lines of code which is responsible just to have those extra things.

Now think about this, as a developer you will be writing multiple methods, right? And you will not write just one method. Every method will have a bit different business logic. So when you say business logic, it will be different for different methods. But what about log code? It will be same. What about security code? It may be same. What about transaction code? It may be same, right? And that too, as a customer what you want is your business logic, right? This is something which you write as a programmer. You don't ask your customer, "Hey, I will be putting all these things," right? And the second thing is, as a developer, we want to see only business logic in the method because if something goes wrong, you don't want to play with this code, right?

## Introducing Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP)

And that's why what is recommended is, let's just imagine if you have 50 to 60 methods, do you think is it logical to write all these things in all the methods? People do that, okay? So when you make the application, we do that if we don't have a choice. But do we have a solution for this? Don't you think we should be making these things common out somewhere?

I mean, I will write this stuff in some other code. And something like this, what I will do here is, I don't want to do all this stuff here. Let me create another class. I will say this class is my... I will call this... anything. I will say `Helper`, helper class. I'll simply say `Helper`. So we got a class here. I want in this class I want all those things. Example, log should be maintained here. So I will say, "Hey, you are responsible to maintain a log." You can write whatever statement you want to write here. Example, I will say `System.out.println` and I will say `logged` or maybe you can say `show called`. You can maintain a log file here. Again, you can write multiple lines of code, that's not important here. You can write, you can do whatever you want. Important is you have to make sure that you separate your code. So whatever extra code you have which is not required in the method, you can separate it out and you can keep that in a separate method, right? So log is done there. We can also do it for security. So what you can do is you can put another method which will maintain the security. And then what you will do is, instead of writing all the code here, you have to call log, right? So you will call log from here, then you will call security from here, right? And then you will call transaction from here. So you will say begin transaction, you will say commit transaction. So you can do all that stuff. But don't you think again, you are calling those methods? So anyway, you have to get the object of Helper, you have to call log.

Now, what if I say you don't have to write any of this code? I mean, you don't have to write any of this code here. Just write about your business logic. So inside your `show()` method, there should only be business logic. You can create all those methods here. Okay, and you don't even have to call them. It will be called automatically. I know you will not believe me here, right?

And that's where AOP comes into picture. Now AOP stands for Aspect-Oriented Programming, which simply means that you have to create—you have to think in a different way. Normally in Java, we use object-oriented programming where everything is an object for us. So I'm not saying you have to replace OOP with AOP, but then AOP is a supplement for AOP which simply means that it supports OOP.

So what we are doing is we are getting a separate class and this class for us will be called as Aspect. In fact, we can also use an annotation here. So we can simply say `@Aspect` and this class becomes an aspect for us. So this aspect will have all the methods which will act as... okay, so we have a special name for those things. So example, we have log, we have transaction, we have security. All these things are actually called as... okay, there are lots of jargons here. Okay, so be with me.

## Adding AOP Dependencies and the @Aspect Annotation

It is also called as cross-cutting concerns because this is something you can take as common, right? So we have all the cross-cutting concerns and you will keep that in an aspect. So whatever cross-cutting concerns you have, you can keep that in an aspect. So you can see I am creating a class here called `Helper` and for me this class is an aspect, and you can simply write `@Aspect` there. Oh, but if I do that, if I say control+space, if I try to import the package, you can see it is not working.

Now the only thing is if you want to use Spring AOP, you have to download the JAR files. Of course, right? With new frameworks you have to download new JAR files. Now if you remember, in Spring Framework we used to work with normal JAR files, right? So whatever Spring Framework required... If you observe, we also have AOP here, so it should work. But then Spring AOP is actually dependent upon some other JAR files. So for that, you have to download those JAR files here. Now from where you will get it? Technically you have to go to Google and download those JAR files, provided you know the JAR file names, because I hate... most of us don't even remember those JAR file names. So what I did is I have downloaded the JAR files for you and in this video's description area, you will find a link where you will find all the JAR files.

Just to show you where it is in my machine, if I open desktop, you can see, ignore all the other things, you can see we have... okay, where is that? We have AOP. In this AOP folder, I have these three files. These three JAR files are something required. Okay? Only if you have these files, only then it will work. So what I'm going to do is I will go back to my NetBeans and here, let me just add those JAR files. So how do you add that? So right-click, again depending upon which IDE you're working with, steps may change. So I will go to Properties and here I will go to Library and I will say Add. And here I will say AOP and I will select all the JAR files, click on Open, and OK. So you can see we got our JAR files. In this, if I expand the library folder here, you can see we got... where is that? If I scroll down, you can see we got these three JAR files and that's it. Now say control+space and you can see it will import the package for you. Our job is done, right? We are importing a package, that's great. Okay.

## Defining Advice and Pointcuts

Now I will go back here. So that we got... we are done with the aspect.

Now, what else is required here? Now the another thing we require is, how will it... how will it be called? Will it be called automatically? Let's try. So what I will do is I will go back to my `SpringDemo`, let's run this code and you can see it prints "Hello world". That's fine, "Hello World" is called because we are calling `alien.show()`, right? That is why "Hello World" is printing, but it is not printing "show called". That means the aspect is not working. This is not getting called automatically.

Now we have to remember some more terms. Some more terms, which is... one of them is called as advice. What is advice? Advice is what. So when you call `show`, what should be called? So what I want is when I call the `show()` method of Alien, when I call the `show()` method of Alien, I want to call this log method. So this is my advice here. And to make it an advice, you have to use the type of advices. There are different types of advices, example you can guess it. I mean, one is `before`. You can guess the next one, which is `after`. You're right. In fact there are five things, we will only discuss about these two. We have `before` and `after`. Before is, this log will be called before calling `show()`. And if you say `after`, this log will be called after calling `show()`. This time I want to go for `before`. So I will say `@Before`, control+space, and you can see we got the package. This is how you define advice. So you will call log before calling the `show()` method and that's what we are doing here. But it is giving you an error.

Now Before says, "I will be getting called, but when?" How would your log know when to be called? Because there are multiple methods, right? Let's say if you're writing an application, you might have 10 methods and you don't want to call log with all the methods. So you can mention here in this round brackets when you have to do it. So you can write in English, you can say, "whenever show method is called." So you can write in English, "whenever a show method gets called," but that will not work, right? That's just normal English. So what you have to provide is... you have to write... okay, there's one more jargon here and that is pointcut. I know, AOP is very simple, the only problem is with the jargons, the technical terms. So your pointcut is something which defines when or where. So at what point you want to call this? So where you want to call this? So I want to call log where? When you execute... So that's how I write it. So you have to say `execution` of the method which is `public void show`. So whenever you call the `show()` method, I want this to be called. Is that easy?

## Enabling AOP and Final Demonstration

Let's go back to my `SpringDemo` and run... oh, it's still not working. You can see we still got "Hello world."

Now, why is it not working? Because you are working with Spring Framework, and Spring Framework says if you are using annotation-based configuration, you have to use one more annotation, which is `@Component`. See, Spring is all about annotations, right? We have to remember so many annotations here. So you have to mention this class is also an annotation. Okay, aspect is also an annotation. Now let's run this, and... oh, it's still not working. You can see it is still not printing "show". It's still not printing "show called".

It's because by default, Aspect AOP is not enabled in your system. Okay? So in your application, you have to make sure that you enable AOP. And how do we do that? So one more annotation, I promise this is the last one. I know that I'm coming with lots of annotations. So this is `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy`. And this is how you do it. So you simply write an annotation which is `EnableAspectJAutoProxy`. Now I think it will work. Let's go back to this `SpringDemo`, let's run this code, and you can see that it worked. We got "show called". Right? And that's the beauty about Spring AOP.

And if you observe in my Alien, you know, this Alien is so innocent. It doesn't even know that you have a Helper class who is doing the log maintenance for you, right? And in future if you want to debug something, you just have to debug this one, right? You don't have to touch the Helper class. And that's the beauty about AOP. So this is the simplest example for AOP. Again, there are lots of things in AOP which we'll discuss later. For the time being, you can try this example. It should work. And let me know your thoughts in the comment section if you have any issues. So that's it from this video. Thanks for watching.
